summary: Describes extensions that let iSCSI run over an RDMA-capable protocol such as iWARP, so data can move directly into SCSI buffers without extra copies. It was replaced by RFC 7145.

eli5.summary: Makes disk-over-network traffic go faster by skipping extra copying. A newer RFC replaced this.

questions: what is iscsi extensions for rdma
how does iser use rdma read and write
what is an stag in rdma
subtitle: How iSCSI storage traffic can run over RDMA so data lands directly in the right memory buffers.

tldr.problem: Traditional iSCSI over TCP must store and reassemble out-of-order segments before placing data, which wastes memory bandwidth, CPU cycles and adds latency at high speeds.
tldr.mechanism: iSER layers iSCSI on an RDMA-Capable Protocol: control PDUs travel as Send messages, and SCSI data moves with RDMA Write and RDMA Read directly into advertised buffers named by STags.
tldr.outcome: Direct data placement works with generic RDMA hardware and software, with iSCSI's login, naming and security reused. RFC 7145 has replaced this document.

today: RFC 5046 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 7145 and updated by RFC 7146, so use those for the current iSER specification.

sections.title: Why iSCSI Needs RDMA
sections.content:
iSCSI (RFC 3720) maps the SCSI architecture onto TCP. Out-of-order TCP segments must be stored and reassembled before the iSCSI layer can place data, because not every segment holds an iSCSI header and TCP has no way to signal message boundaries. At high speeds the RFC calls this counter-productive: it wastes memory bandwidth, reassembly memory and CPU cycles, and adds store-and-forward latency.

RFC 3720 offered optional "markers" for this, but most implementations do not support them, so marker-based direct placement is unusable in practice. The iWARP stack gives direct data placement that is usable, and InfiniBand offers similar functions. The generic term for such stacks is RDMA-Capable Protocol (RCaP). iSER (iSCSI Extensions for RDMA) lets iSCSI use them through a generic RDMA-Capable Controller.
sections.eli5: Normally data arrives in a jumble and has to be sorted and copied before it is used. RDMA lets the data go straight to the right spot.

sections.title: Design Goals and Layering
sections.content:
The goals include direct in-order or out-of-order placement of SCSI data into pre-allocated buffers while keeping in-order delivery, no major changes to the SCSI Architecture Model, reuse of the iSCSI ecosystem (naming, discovery, negotiation, security), and use of generic RDMA-Capable Controllers or a software-only implementation. If either side does not support iSER, the session falls back to Traditional iSCSI.

iSER sits between the iSCSI layer and the RCaP layer. For TCP the RCaP is iWARP (RDMAP, DDP and MPA); for InfiniBand it is the Reliable Connected Transport Service. Because RCaP ensures data integrity, iSCSI header and data digests are negotiated to None for iSCSI/iSER sessions.
sections.eli5: iSER is a middle layer. It lets the old storage rules keep working while a faster delivery system does the carrying.

sections.title: How Data Moves: Send, RDMA Write and RDMA Read
sections.content:
A Steering Tag (STag) identifies an I/O buffer. The initiator advertises a buffer by putting its STag in the iSER header of the message carrying the SCSI Command PDU. The base Tagged Offset is always assumed to be zero.

Control-type PDUs, such as commands and responses, travel in Send messages. Data-type PDUs use RDMA operations driven by the target. For a SCSI read, the target uses RDMA Writes to place data in the initiator's buffer. For a SCSI write, the target uses RDMA Reads to fetch the data. The initiator itself uses neither RDMA Writes nor RDMA Reads.

The target returns the SCSI Response PDU in a SendInvSE message, which automatically invalidates the advertised STag on normal completion. Bidirectional commands and abnormal completions are exceptions, and then the initiator must invalidate the STag explicitly.
sections.eli5: The person who wants the data holds up a numbered tray. The storage side then puts data on the tray, or picks up data from it, without being asked again, and the tray is retired when the job is done.

sections.title: Login and the iSER Hello Exchange
sections.content:
Login happens as in RFC 3720, on the same connection that later runs iSER. iSER-assisted mode is negotiated with the key RDMAExtensions=Yes, which both sides must exchange on the leading connection. The default is No, and it MUST NOT be negotiated for a Discovery session. It is a session-wide attribute: if negotiated to Yes on the leading connection, all later connections of the session use iSER-assisted mode. When it is Yes, HeaderDigest and DataDigest MUST be negotiated to None.

After the switch, the first iSER message from the initiator MUST be the iSER Hello, declaring its iSER-IRD value. The target's first message MUST be the HelloReply, declaring iSER-ORD, which is the minimum of its own value and the initiator's IRD. It is a negotiation failure if the initiator's IRD is greater than 0 while the target's ORD is 0, or if the supported iSER protocol versions do not overlap.
sections.eli5: Both sides first agree, during the normal check-in, to use the fast lane. Then they swap a short hello that says how many pick-ups at once each side can handle.

sections.title: The iSER Header
sections.content:
Every Send message carries an iSER header in the first 12 bytes of its payload. The 4-bit opcode says which kind: 0001b for an iSCSI control-type PDU, 0010b for Hello and 0011b for HelloReply. Other opcodes are reserved.

For a control-type PDU, the header has two flags, WSV and RSV, saying whether the 32-bit Write STag and Read STag fields are valid. The Write STag advertises the buffer holding data for a SCSI write, and is used as the data source in the target's RDMA Read operations. The Read STag advertises the buffer for a SCSI read, and is used as the data sink for RDMA Writes. Invalid STag fields MUST be zero, and reserved bits MUST be zero on transmit and ignored on reception.

The Hello message carries MaxVer, MinVer and a 16-bit iSER-IRD. The HelloReply carries a REJ flag, MaxVer, CurVer and a 16-bit iSER-ORD. Versions MUST be set to one.
sections.eli5: Each message starts with a short note saying what kind it is, and, when needed, the numbers of the trays where data should go or come from.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of iSER is that of the underlying RCaP layer. For iWARP it is covered in the RDMAP and DDP security documents. Because iSER-assisted iSCSI is still iSCSI, all the iSCSI security requirements from RFC 3720 and RFC 3723 apply. If IPsec is used, it MUST be established before the connection moves to iSER-assisted mode.

To limit denial-of-service attacks, the iSCSI layer MUST NOT ask iSER to allocate RCaP connection resources until the Login Phase is far enough along that the peer is reasonably unlikely to be an attacker.
sections.eli5: The same locks that protected the old way still apply. And you do not set out lots of chairs for a visitor until you have checked they are not a troublemaker.
